clinicalPearls: Swelling over the point of the elbow from inflammation of the superficial olecranon bursa
Causes include repetitive pressure and friction, direct trauma, crystal arthropathy such as gout, and infection
The key clinical task is distinguishing septic from aseptic bursitis
Warmth, marked erythema, fever, disproportionate pain and an overlying skin breach favour a septic bursa
Aspiration with fluid sent for cell count, Gram stain, culture and crystal microscopy is central when infection is suspected
Aseptic bursitis is generally managed conservatively with avoidance of pressure, and aspiration if symptomatic
Corticosteroid injection is reserved for stubborn aseptic cases and avoided when infection is possible because of complication risk
Septic bursitis requires antibiotics and sometimes drainage
reference.pathophysiology: The olecranon bursa is a superficial sac over the extensor aspect of the elbow that reduces friction between the skin and the olecranon. Repetitive pressure or leaning on the elbow, a direct blow, or systemic conditions such as gout and rheumatoid arthritis can provoke bursal inflammation and effusion. Because it is superficial, the bursa is prone to becoming infected, commonly through a breach in the overlying skin and most often with skin flora such as staphylococci. Distinguishing this septic process from aseptic inflammation is the central diagnostic challenge.
additionalDifferentials: Olecranon fracture or other elbow trauma
additionalInvestigations: Bursal aspiration with fluid cell count, Gram stain and culture
Polarised light microscopy of the aspirate for crystals
Inflammatory markers, with blood cultures if systemically unwell
Serum urate where gout is suspected, recognising its limits in the acute phase
Plain radiographs if fracture, foreign body or bony spur is suspected
Ultrasound to characterise the fluid collection
redFlags: Fever, spreading erythema and disproportionate pain suggesting septic bursitis or cellulitis
An overlying skin breach or immunosuppression increasing infection risk
Failure to settle, raising suspicion of infection or underlying disease
reference.prognosis: Aseptic bursitis usually settles with conservative care, although it can recur with continued pressure; septic bursitis generally resolves with prompt antibiotics and drainage but may need repeated aspiration.
pitfalls: Injecting corticosteroid into a bursa that may be infected
Failing to aspirate and analyse fluid when infection is possible
Missing gout as an underlying cause
Attributing a fracture-related swelling to simple bursitis
references: Brukner and Khan's Clinical Sports Medicine
management: Distinguish septic from aseptic bursitis by bursal aspiration for cell count, Gram stain, culture and crystal microscopy to direct treatment

Septic bursitis treated with antistaphylococcal antibiotics such as flucloxacillin covering skin flora, together with drainage or aspiration, and incision and drainage or bursectomy for refractory cases
Aseptic bursitis managed conservatively with avoidance of pressure and leaning, elbow padding, rest, ice and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs
Aspiration of symptomatic aseptic effusions, generally avoiding corticosteroid injection especially where infection cannot be excluded
Treat the underlying cause, with urate-lowering and anti-inflammatory therapy for gout and disease control for rheumatoid arthritis
Follow-up for recurrence with continued pressure, reserving bursectomy for recurrent or chronic disease
